name: EMS suit / electrical muscle stimulation

lead: EMS uses electrical pulses to trigger muscle contractions, and whole-body suits do this across many muscles during a workout. People use them hoping for a more toned, muscular look on top of or in place of regular training.

Pulses through skin electrodes make motor nerves fire so muscle fibers contract, and are said to recruit fast-twitch fibers. EMS is established in rehabilitation, and small trials in healthy adults exist, but none found here measure muscle appearance.

paras: Whole-body suits are used in short, supervised studio sessions where electrodes across the body deliver pulses while the person does light movements. Individual electrode pads are also used on single muscles. Results, if any, build over repeated sessions.

Skin irritation and burns are listed adverse effects. Pacemakers and several other conditions are contraindications, and a case of rhabdomyolysis after a whole-body EMS session has been reported. People with implanted devices or medical conditions should check with a clinician.

angle.text: Whole-body EMS suits are sold for toning on the idea that stimulated contractions add a muscle stimulus and a more muscular look. EMS is established in rehabilitation and small fitness trials exist, but none measure appearance.

lead: Electrical muscle stimulation (EMS, also called NMES or electromyostimulation) uses electrical impulses delivered through skin electrodes to make muscles contract. It is used in rehabilitation, athletic training and consumer fitness.[1] Whole-body EMS (WB-EMS) suits and vests place electrodes across many muscle groups at once and are sold in studios and for home use as a short, low-impact way to train.

People use EMS to look better by adding stimulus to the muscles that shape the physique: the idea is that the contractions add to or stand in for part of a workout, helping build or maintain muscle size, firmness and tone in the abs, arms, glutes and legs. Fitness studios commonly offer brief supervised WB-EMS sessions, and individual pads and abdominal belts are sold for home use.

Randomized trials of whole-body EMS in healthy adults exist, including a 6-week trial in 64 healthy university students and a 6-week trial in 24 young women with overweight or higher BMI.[2][3] A systematic review of electrical stimulation and strength in healthy adults examined ten studies with 174 participants.[4] A Danish case report describes rhabdomyolysis after a whole-body session.[5] No trial found measures muscle appearance as the main outcome, although the young-women trial recorded body composition, waist and hip circumference and abdominal MRI as secondary measures.[3]

paras: Luigi Galvani provided early evidence in 1761 that electric current can activate muscle. Through the 19th and 20th centuries researchers documented the electrical properties behind muscle movement and found that stimulation caused long-term changes in muscle.[1]

In the 1960s Soviet sport scientists used EMS with elite athletes and reported force gains of around 40 percent; the findings were shared with Western sport bodies in the 1970s, but results there conflicted, partly because the mechanisms were poorly understood.[1] Whole-body systems with wireless electrodes and vests later moved EMS into commercial fitness studios; a 2018 study notes that WB-EMS had been upgraded and had overcome the limitations of earlier systems but lacked specific application guidelines.[2]

Consumer and studio EMS comes in several formats. Single-muscle pads and abdominal belts apply current over one area such as the abs or quadriceps, and wearable units are marketed for home use.[1][6] Whole-body suits and vests place conductive electrode pads over the chest, back, abdomen, arms, glutes and legs, and the 2018 trial authors describe a suit that replaced water-soaked garments with silicone conductive pads and used wireless Bluetooth control with a stated range of up to 40 metres.[2] Studios typically run supervised sessions in which the wearer performs simple movements such as squats, lunges, crunches or planks while the current is on.[2][3]

EMS is distinguished from TENS, which uses current mainly for pain relief rather than to drive contraction.[1] In the US, devices are cleared either over the counter for muscle toning or by prescription for therapy.[1][6]

EMS delivers impulses through skin pads near target muscles that imitate the action potentials normally sent by the central nervous system, triggering involuntary contractions. Wikipedia reports that NMES stimulates muscle fibres directly and also activates corticomotor pathways, is said to recruit fast-twitch fibres, and can drive neural adaptations resembling those from high-intensity voluntary exercise.[1] Protocols aimed at fatigue resistance build endurance, while others increase force production, so adaptations depend on the stimulation pattern.[1]
Whole-body suits place electrode pads over the chest, back, abdomen, arms, glutes and legs so several muscle groups contract together, in contrast with TENS units used for pain relief.[1]

EMS is used to limit muscle atrophy during inactivity or injury, and as a training adjunct in healthy people.[1] A Cochrane review cited by Wikipedia found quadriceps strength gains in people with advanced disease but graded the evidence low certainty. Reports describe benefits in haemodialysis patients, after stroke, after knee surgery and in critical illness, while benefit in patellofemoral pain remains uncertain.[1] Trials in other settings include a randomized trial of in-bed cycling with quadriceps stimulation in critically ill adults[7] and an 8-week study combining frequency-specific EMS with resistance training for muscle mass, strength and body composition in men and women, described as a feasibility and safety study.[8]

Wikipedia describes EMS as more helpful before exercise and as ineffective for recovery afterward, with a possible increase in muscle soreness. It describes calorie burn from EMS as marginal and notes that the FDA does not certify devices claiming weight reduction.[1]

In the US, over-the-counter EMS devices can be marketed only for muscle toning, while prescription devices serve therapeutic purposes such as preventing disuse atrophy and muscle re-education. FDA import guidance treats claims of girth reduction, weight reduction, cellulite removal and spot reducing as misbranding.[1] The FTC has acted against consumer EMS devices with unsubstantiated claims, including a 2002 action involving three top-selling electronic abdominal exercise belts; many such products left the market and some later obtained FDA certification.[1]

Wikipedia reports a 2009 FDA import alert stating that stimulators are misbranded if they claim girth reduction, weight reduction, cellulite removal or spot reducing, and states that the FDA rejects certification of devices claiming weight reduction.[6] The FTC press release cited there, dated May 2002, charged three top-selling electronic abdominal exercise belts with making false claims.[6]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and fitness culture
paras: EMS appears in appearance and fitness discussions as a way to train the abs, glutes and arms in short sessions, and as a supplement for people who find it hard to get to a gym. A Hacker News thread from 2021 shows one person's account of doing EMS in place of gym sessions; a commenter described the write-up as lacking objective strength measures, and the author replied that they had not yet found a way to measure objectively.[9] A 2023 Hacker News post linked a Wall Street Journal piece on whole-body EMS, but drew no discussion.[9]

Trial authors describe whole-body suits as marketed as time-saving and as allowing stronger contractions and more efficient exercise, while noting that evidence in healthy people is mixed and that most earlier studies were in elderly or patient groups.[3]

Listed contraindications include pacemakers, fractures, burns, skin lesions, lupus erythematosus and thromboembolic disease including deep vein thrombosis. FDA-mandated warnings advise against use on the carotid sinus, across the chest or across the brain, and caution in pregnancy. Skin irritation and burns are the adverse effects listed.[1]
A 2023 case report describes rhabdomyolysis, a breakdown of muscle tissue, in a young woman after whole-body electromyostimulation training.[5]

Whole-body suits. A double-blind randomized trial at a Korean university (2017) assigned 64 healthy students aged 20 to 25 to wear a suit with stimulation or without it for six weeks, with 20-minute sessions three times a week of ten isometric exercises such as squats, planks and bridges at about 80 percent of the maximum tolerable intensity.[2] Graded exercise tests showed lower systolic blood pressure and higher oxygen uptake in the stimulated group at several stages; no participants dropped out, five reported chest tightness or discomfort, and the authors suggested leaving the chest area out of future suits. They also noted that WB-EMS has been linked to muscle damage and rhabdomyolysis risk in other reports.[2]

A second trial randomized 24 young women with BMI of 23 or higher to the same low-intensity resistance exercises (squats, lunges, crunches, planks) for six weeks, three 20-minute sessions a week, with current switched on in only one group.[3] It measured body composition, waist and hip circumference, lipid profile, abdominal MRI cross-sectional area, knee strength and balance. Weight, muscle mass, fat mass and BMI did not differ significantly between groups; knee-flexor strength at one speed and one balance measure improved only in the suit group; waist and hip measurements fell in both groups, and rectus abdominis area increased in both with no significant difference between them. The authors listed the small sample, short duration and uncontrolled diet as limitations, and the suit's manufacturer funded the study.[3]

A pilot study with eight male Paralympic-level athletes with disabilities wore a suit for hour-long sessions twice a week for eight weeks, targeting the chest and triceps, and recorded higher muscle activity in several muscle groups and higher oxygen uptake and energy expenditure afterwards; it had no control group.[10] An 8-week randomized feasibility and safety study combined frequency-specific EMS with resistance training and measured muscle mass, strength and body composition.[8]

Systematic review. A review of published studies from 2008 to 2020 on EMS and strength gains in healthy adults included ten studies with 174 subjects, eight on lower-limb muscles and two on the elbow flexors, five with concurrent voluntary resistance training, and noted heterogeneous protocols.[4] In clinical settings, a JAMA 2018 randomized trial tested in-bed leg cycling with quadriceps stimulation in critically ill adults.[7] Wikipedia notes a 2016 Cochrane review that found low-certainty evidence of quadriceps strength gains in people with advanced disease.[6]
No trials measuring muscle size or visible appearance as the primary outcome of a whole-body suit were found.

lore.intro: Community material on EMS suits is sparse; it appears in a few Hacker News posts by people trying EMS in place of gym sessions, and most discussion of EMS in online fitness circles concerns whether the contraction can stand in for lifting.[9][9]
